# Before we start

These exercises continue with data import. We look at a file where the parser guesses wrong, at
an Excel file with a typo hidden in one cell, and at JSON data that we load straight from the
web.

Write your code in an R script saved in `2026_Data_Handling/exercises/code`, for example
`exercise_04.R`. Open your RStudio project first, so that every path starting with `data/`
works. Type the code rather than copying it, and read every error message. If something does
not work, raise your hand.

| Exercise | What we do |
|------|------------------------------------------------|
| 1 | When the parser guesses wrong: `challenge.csv` |
| 2 | Importing an Excel file and finding the problem |
| 3 | Fixing the problem and writing the data back to disk |
| 4 | JSON from the web: import without clicking and saving |
| 5 | From nested JSON to a rectangular table |

**The data.** We use one file, `airquality_data.xlsx`. Download it from the course repository,
folder `materialsExercises/04_data_import/data`, and save it in your own `data` folder. The
other two data sets come with R (`challenge.csv`, a file shipped with the `readr` package) and
from the web (Exercise 4).

The Excel file contains the New York air quality measurements from May to September 1973, one
row per day, with ozone, solar radiation, wind and temperature. It is the `airquality` data
set that ships with R, to which we added a mistake.

# Exercise 1: when the parser guesses wrong

`readr` guesses the type of every column from the values it sees. Most of the time that works.
In this exercise we look at what happens when it does not. The example file `challenge.csv`
is part of the `readr` package, and the chapter on data import in R for Data Science
(<https://r4ds.had.co.nz/data-import.html>, Sections 11.1 to 11.4) is built on it.

1. Import the file and look at what you got:

```{r eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
library(readr)

challenge <- read_csv(readr_example("challenge.csv"))
head(challenge)
spec(challenge)
```

   How many rows and columns are there, and which type did `readr` assign to `x` and to `y`?

2. Look at the rows around the first thousand, where the content of the columns changes:

```{r eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
challenge$x[c(1:5, 998:1003)]
challenge$y[c(1:5, 998:1003)]
```

   What do the first rows of `y` contain, and what do the later ones contain? Explain why a
   parser that looks only at the beginning of a file could get the type of `y` wrong.

3. Reproduce the problem. Tell `readr` that `x` is a double and `y` is a logical, and ask for
   the problems:

```{r eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
challenge_wrong <- read_csv(
  readr_example("challenge.csv"),
  col_types = cols(x = col_double(), y = col_logical())
)
problems(challenge_wrong)
```

   How many problems are reported? Read the columns `row`, `expected` and `actual`: what did
   the parser expect, and what did it find?

4. Now state the correct type for `y` yourself, and check the result:

```{r eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
challenge_fixed <- read_csv(
  readr_example("challenge.csv"),
  col_types = cols(x = col_double(), y = col_date())
)
tail(challenge_fixed)
sum(is.na(challenge_fixed$y))
```

5. In older versions of `readr` the default call in question 1 produced the problem of
   question 3. What does your version do, and why does this not make the exercise useless?

# Exercise 2: importing an Excel file

1. Import the file with `read_excel()` from the `readxl` package:

```{r eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
library(readxl)

airquality_data <- read_excel("data/airquality_data.xlsx")
```

2. Familiarise yourself with the data with `print()`, `dim()` and `str()`. How many rows and
   columns are there, and what do the columns measure?

3. Look at the `type` of each column in the output of `print()`. One column has a type that
   does not fit what it contains. Which one, and what type would you expect?

4. Count the missing values in every column:

```{r eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
colSums(is.na(airquality_data))
```

   Which columns have missing values? Is a missing value in `Ozone` a problem in the same
   sense as the problem in question 3?

5. Find the cause of the wrong type. Look at the distinct values of the column:

```{r eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
sort(unique(airquality_data$Month))
```

   Which value does not belong, and in which row is it? Why did one cell change the type of the
   whole column?

# Exercise 3: fixing the problem and writing the data back

1. Replace the wrong value with the number it stands for. Do it in a copy of the data, so that
   you can always go back to the original:

```{r eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
airquality_fixed <- airquality_data
airquality_fixed$Month[airquality_fixed$Month == "five"] <- "5"
```

   Print the column again. Is the problem solved?

2. The column is still text. Convert it to a number and check the type:

```{r eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
airquality_fixed$Month <- as.numeric(airquality_fixed$Month)
str(airquality_fixed)
```

   What would `as.numeric()` have done to the cell `"five"` if you had skipped question 1? Why
   is that worse than the error we started from?

3. Check that the repair worked: how many observations are there per month, and how many days
   does each of the five months have in reality?

4. Save the repaired data set as `airquality_data_fixed.xlsx` with `write_xlsx()` from the
   `writexl` package, and open the file in Excel to look at the result.

5. Write the whole solution in an R script. Document in comments why the problem occurs and
   how you solved it.

6. Could you have fixed the problem at import, without touching the data afterwards? Look at
   the argument `col_types` of `read_excel()`. What happens with `col_types = "numeric"` for
   `Month`, and what would you have to check afterwards?

# Exercise 4: JSON from the web

JSON is a format for data that is not rectangular, and many web services deliver it. We use
the data of the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) on COVID-19 cases
worldwide, published through the EU Open Data Portal.

1. Visit the EU Open Data Portal at <https://data.europa.eu/> and find the data set "COVID-19
   Cases Worldwide". Which formats does the portal offer?

2. Download the data in JSON format, but do not click and save. Load the data directly into R
   from the web. The direct link to the JSON file is
   <https://opendata.ecdc.europa.eu/covid19/casedistribution/json/>. The package to use is
   `jsonlite`:

```{r eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
library(jsonlite)

url_covid19 <- "https://opendata.ecdc.europa.eu/covid19/casedistribution/json/"
data_json <- fromJSON(txt = url_covid19)
```

3. Why is it better to read data from a URL in the script than to download a file by hand? What
   can go wrong with this approach?

# Exercise 5: from nested JSON to a rectangular table

1. Look at the object `fromJSON()` returned, with `class()`, `names()` and `str(max.level =
   1)`. Is it a data frame?

2. Extract the data frame from the list, once by position and once by name:

```{r eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
covid <- data_json[[1]]
covid <- data_json$records
```

   Which of the two is more robust if the provider adds a second element to the list?

3. Check that the result is rectangular: each record is a row, each field a column. How many
   rows and columns are there, and which type does each column have?

4. The columns `day`, `month` and `year` are text. Build a proper date from `dateRep` with
   `as.Date()` and find out which period the data covers. Which format string do you need?

5. Which country has the largest number of reported cases on a single day, and on which day?
   Use `which.max()`.

# Additional exercises for training

::: {.callout-note}
Exercise 6 uses what we did in Exercises 2 and 3 on another data set. Do it at home, the
solution is published with the rest.
:::

## Exercise 6: a second Excel file

1. Write a function `check_types(df)` that takes a data frame and returns the names of the
   columns of type character.

2. Apply it to `airquality_data`. Which columns does it report, and which of them are
   expected to be text?

3. Extend the function so that it also reports, for each text column, the values that cannot
   be converted to a number. Hint: `suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x))` returns `NA` for those
   values, and `is.na()` finds them.

4. Why is a check like this worth writing as a function rather than running by hand once?
